title: She wasn’t supposed to make it into the story.
paragraphs: She wasn’t supposed to make it into the story.
Not someone like her.
Her name carried a reputation long before it carried redemption. In the streets of Jericho, people knew exactly who Rahab was. And it wasn’t something you’d want written next to your name.
A prostitute.
That label alone should have disqualified her from anything holy. From anything God-related. From anything eternal.
But it didn’t.
And that’s exactly where the tension begins.
Because somewhere deep down, you’ve believed the same lie she could have believed—that your past has already decided your future.
But here’s what most people don’t realize…
God doesn’t start where people start.

People begin with your history.
God begins with your heart.
Rahab lived inside a city marked for destruction. Book of Joshua makes it clear—Jericho was under judgment. Not partially. Completely.
Everything in it was doomed.
Including her.
And if we’re honest, that’s where your story intersects with hers more than you’d like to admit. Because Scripture doesn’t divide humanity into “good people” and “bad people.”
It divides us into the guilty… and the forgiven.
“For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.” — Epistle to the Romans 3:23
Read that again.
All.
Rahab’s sin was visible. Yours might be hidden. But before a holy God, exposure isn’t the issue.
Guilt is.
God saw it.
You knew.
And still… something shifted in her.
When the spies of Israel entered Jericho, Rahab did something that didn’t make sense on the surface. She hid them. Protected them. Risked her life for them.
Why?
Because she believed something.
“I know that the Lord has given you the land… for the Lord your God, He is God in heaven above and on earth beneath.” — Joshua 2:9–11
That wasn’t just information.
That was faith breaking through a corrupted life.
She had heard about the power of God—the crossing of the Red Sea, the victories of Israel—and while the rest of Jericho hardened in fear, she softened in belief.
Same evidence.
Different response.
That’s where everything changes.
Because salvation has never been about having a clean past.
It has always been about responding rightly to God.
“By faith Rahab the prostitute did not perish… because she had given a friendly welcome to the spies.” — Epistle to the Hebrews 11:31
Did you catch that?
Scripture does not erase her past title.
It says “Rahab the prostitute.”
And still… saved.
Not because her sin didn’t matter.
But because her faith was real.
That tension is the Gospel.
You don’t get to rewrite your past.
But Jesus rewrites your ending.
Rahab didn’t negotiate her way into salvation. She didn’t promise to become better first. She didn’t clean herself up and then ask God to accept her.
She believed.
And that belief produced action.
She tied a scarlet cord in her window—a visible sign of her trust in God’s promise. When judgment came crashing down on Jericho, one house stood untouched.
Hers.
Not because she deserved it.
But because she trusted the One who saves.
And here’s where it gets even deeper…
She didn’t just survive.
She was brought in.
Rahab became part of Israel. She married into the people of God. And generations later, her name appears again—not in shame, but in legacy.
“The book of the genealogy of Jesus Christ…” — Gospel of Matthew 1:1
And there she is.
Rahab.
In the bloodline of Jesus.
Let that settle.
A woman once defined by sin becomes part of the story that brings salvation to the world.
That’s not coincidence.
That’s grace.
“But God shows His love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.” — Romans 5:8
Not after you fix yourself.
Not after you prove yourself.
While you were still in it.
That’s where Jesus steps in.
So why was Rahab saved despite her past?
Because her past wasn’t stronger than God’s mercy.
Because her faith was louder than her history.
Because God responds to repentance, not reputation.
And now you’re standing in the same tension she stood in.
You know enough.
You’ve heard enough.
The question isn’t whether God can save someone like you.
Rahab already answered that.
The real question is…
Will you believe Him enough to respond?
Because there are only two directions from here.
You either cling to your past and fall with it…
Or you surrender to Christ and rise beyond it.
No middle ground.
That’s not emotion.
That’s exposure.
Say it plainly if you feel it:
“I’ve been hiding, but I believe.”
Or even simpler:
“I need that mercy.”
Let it come out of you.
Follow this path if you’re done playing with surface-level faith and want truth that actually transforms you, corrects you, and pulls you deeper into what God is really saying.
There’s more waiting, but not forever.
